description: Listen to teachers, classmates, and short talks about school, math, science, and our community, then show what you understood.

A.studentGoal: I can listen for important words and choose the matching answer.

info.headline: Catch the key words you hear.
info.summary: Level A is for students who are just starting to learn English. You will hear one to three short, slow sentences about your classroom, math, science, and stories. Pictures and emoji help you understand. You listen for key words like names, numbers, places, and feelings, and then choose the answer that matches.
canDo: I can follow a short classroom direction.
I can find a place or thing when I hear its name and a place word.
I can catch numbers and math words like "in all" and "more."
I can put two or three story events in order with first, next, and then.

categories.title: Follow Class Directions
categories.desc: Listen to a teacher's direction and find the place or the things you need.

categories.title: Math and Science Words
categories.desc: Catch key math and science words: equal parts, roots, in all, more.

categories.title: Who, What, and Where
categories.desc: Listen for details about weather, animals, and community helpers.

categories.title: Short Stories
categories.desc: Listen to a short story and tell what happened and how someone feels.

activities.title: Where Does the Book Go?
activities.skill: Following a one-step classroom direction with place words
activities.directions: Look at the picture of the classroom. Listen to your teacher. Then choose the place the teacher talks about.
activities.prompt: Where does the teacher want you to put the book?

picture.alt: A classroom with a window and a bookshelf under it, a whiteboard, a teacher's desk, cubbies by the door, and a round reading rug on the floor.

activities.script: Please put your book on the shelf. The shelf is under the window.

options.text: On the shelf under the window
In a cubby by the door

vocabulary: a flat board where we keep books and things
estante: tabla plana donde guardamos libros y cosas
debajo de: más abajo que otra cosa
glass in the wall that lets light in
ventana: vidrio en la pared que deja entrar la luz
activities.correct: Yes! You heard "shelf" and "under the window." Two clues helped you find the place.
activities.hint: Listen for the name of a thing in the room. Then listen for a place word like "under."
activities.support: Point to the window in the picture. Now look below it. What do you see there?
activities.extension: Tell a partner where to put a pencil. Use a place word: on, under, or next to.
wida: Inform: identify a place from a spoken direction

teacher.use: Use in the first weeks for newcomers learning classroom routines and place words.
teacher.function: Follow a one-step oral direction; locate objects with place words.
teacher.lower: Read twice and point to the window while you say it. Accept pointing as the answer.
teacher.onLevel: Read once at a slow, clear pace.
teacher.challenge: Give a two-step direction: put the book on the shelf, then sit on the rug.
teacher.noTech: Print the classroom picture. Students place a paper book cut-out where you say.
teacher.prompt: Which two words helped you find the place?

activities.title: What Do You Need for Math?
activities.skill: Listening for needed items in a direction
activities.directions: Listen to your teacher. Choose ALL the things you need. There is more than one answer.
activities.prompt: What do you need for math today?
activities.script: For math today, you need a pencil and a ruler. You do not need crayons.
vocabulary: a tool to measure how long something is
regla: herramienta para medir qué tan largo es algo
no: palabras que dicen que algo no pasa
activities.correct: Great listening! You need a pencil and a ruler. You also caught "do not need crayons."
activities.hint: Listen for "you need." Then listen for "do not need." Those words tell you what to leave.
activities.support: Hold up a pencil and a ruler. Say: I need a pencil. I need a ruler. I do not need crayons.
activities.extension: Tell a partner two things you need for reading time.
wida: Inform: identify items named in a direction

teacher.use: Morning routine or math launch for Level 1 students.
teacher.function: Identify items named in an oral direction; notice negation.
teacher.lower: Show real supplies on the table. Students touch each one as you say it.
teacher.onLevel: Read once; students choose both items.
teacher.challenge: Add a third item and a second "do not" to track.
teacher.noTech: Students hold up the real supplies they hear.
teacher.prompt: What word told you NOT to take something?

activities.title: Find Amir on the Playground
activities.skill: Locating a person with place words
activities.directions: Look at the picture of the playground. Listen. Then choose where Amir is.
activities.prompt: Where is Amir?

picture.alt: A playground with a slide, swings, a big tree, and a bench. A child plays at each place.

activities.script: This is my friend Amir. He is under the big tree. He likes the shade.
vocabulary: debajo de: más abajo que otra cosa
a tall plant with a trunk and leaves
árbol: planta alta con tronco y hojas
a cool, dark place out of the sun
sombra: lugar fresco donde no llega el sol
activities.correct: Yes! Amir is under the big tree. The word "shade" was another clue: trees make shade.
activities.hint: Listen for a place word: on, under, or next to. Then listen for the thing.
activities.support: Point to each place in the picture and say its name with your teacher: slide, swings, tree, bench.
activities.extension: Choose another child in the picture. Tell a partner where that child is.
wida: Inform: locate a person using place words

teacher.use: Use with the playground picture to practice place words and recess vocabulary.
teacher.function: Locate a person or object from an oral description.
teacher.lower: Read twice. Point to the tree while saying "under the big tree."
teacher.onLevel: Read once at a slow pace.
teacher.challenge: Students describe where another child is; a partner points.
teacher.noTech: Print the picture; students put a counter on the place they hear.
teacher.prompt: What place word did you hear?

activities.title: Which Circle Did You Hear?
activities.skill: Matching a spoken fraction description to a model
activities.directions: Listen to your teacher describe a circle. Choose the matching circle.
activities.prompt: Which picture shows the circle the teacher describes?
activities.script: This circle has four equal parts. Three parts are shaded.

picture.alt: A circle cut into four equal parts. One part is shaded.
A circle cut into six equal parts. Three parts are shaded.
A circle cut into four equal parts. Two parts are shaded.
A circle cut into four equal parts. Three parts are shaded.

vocabulary: pieces that are all the same size
partes iguales: pedazos que tienen el mismo tamaño
a number that names part of a whole
fracción: número que nombra una parte de un entero
frames: ___ parts are shaded. That is three fourths.
activities.correct: Yes! Four equal parts and three are shaded. That is the fraction three fourths.
activities.hint: You need TWO numbers: how many parts in all, and how many are shaded.
activities.support: Count with your finger: how many parts in each circle? Find the circles with 4 parts first.
activities.extension: Draw a circle with four equal parts. Shade one part. Tell a partner: One part is shaded.
wida: Inform: match a description to a math model
Language of Math: equal parts, shaded

teacher.use: Grade 3 fractions: connect spoken fraction language to area models.
teacher.function: Process two quantities in an oral description to identify a model.
teacher.lower: Read twice. Hold up four fingers, then three, as you read.
teacher.onLevel: Read once; ask students to say the fraction name after answering.
teacher.challenge: Students describe a circle for a partner to draw.
teacher.noTech: Draw the four circles on the board; students point.
teacher.prompt: Why is Circle 2 not the answer, even with three shaded parts?

activities.title: The Part That Drinks Water
activities.skill: Identifying a plant part from its job
activities.directions: Look at the picture of the plant. Listen to the clue. Choose the plant part.
activities.prompt: Which part of the plant is the teacher talking about?

picture.alt: A plant growing in the soil, with roots under the ground, a green stem, leaves, and a yellow flower on top.

activities.script: This part of the plant is under the ground. It takes in water from the soil.
vocabulary: plant parts under the ground that take in water
raíces: partes de la planta bajo la tierra que toman agua
suelo: tierra donde crecen las plantas
activities.correct: Correct! The roots are under the ground and take in water from the soil.
activities.hint: Listen for WHERE the part is: "under the ground." Look at the bottom of the picture.
activities.support: Point to each part in the picture with your teacher: flower, leaves, stem, roots.
activities.extension: Choose another part. Tell its job: The leaves ___.
wida: Inform: identify a plant part from its location and job

teacher.use: Science: plant parts and their jobs (grades 3–4 life science).
teacher.function: Identify a part from a spoken description of location and function.
teacher.lower: Read twice; trace the line from the soil to the roots.
teacher.challenge: Give a clue for the leaves (they use sunlight to make food) and have students answer.
teacher.noTech: Bring a real plant with roots showing; students point.
teacher.prompt: What clue told you where the part is?

activities.title: What Is the Weather?
activities.skill: Matching a weather report to a symbol
activities.directions: Listen to the weather for today. Choose the matching weather.
activities.prompt: Which picture shows the weather today?
activities.script: Today it is cold and windy. Please wear your jacket at recess.
vocabulary: with a lot of moving air
a coat you wear to stay warm
activities.correct: Yes! Cold and windy. The jacket was a clue that it is cold.
activities.hint: Listen for two weather words joined by "and."
activities.support: Act it out: shiver for cold, wave your arms for wind. Which symbol matches?
activities.extension: Tell a partner what to wear on a rainy day.
wida: Inform: identify weather words in a short report

teacher.use: Morning meeting weather routine.
teacher.function: Match spoken weather words to symbols.
teacher.lower: Act out each weather word with gestures before reading.
teacher.challenge: Ask: Is snowy also cold? Why is it not the answer?
teacher.noTech: Hold up weather cards; students point.
teacher.prompt: What did the teacher say to wear? Why?

activities.title: Lucía's Morning
activities.skill: Putting three spoken steps in order
activities.directions: Listen to Lucía's morning at school. Put the steps in order.
activities.prompt: What does Lucía do first, next, and then?
activities.script: First, Lucía hangs up her backpack. Next, she eats breakfast. Then, she reads a book.
vocabulary: primero: antes que todos los demás
a bag you carry on your back
mochila: bolsa que llevas en la espalda
activities.correct: Great! First the backpack, next breakfast, then a book. Order words helped you.
activities.hint: Listen for first, next, and then. Each one starts a new step.
activities.support: Hold up one finger for first, two for next, three for then while you listen again.
activities.extension: Tell your own morning with first, next, and then.
wida: Narrate: retell events in order using first, next, then

teacher.use: Use to teach sequence words with a familiar school routine.
teacher.function: Sequence events in a short oral narrative.
teacher.lower: Read twice; students hold up fingers for each step.
teacher.challenge: Add a fourth step (she says hello to her teacher).
teacher.noTech: Use three picture cards; students line them up.
teacher.prompt: Which word told you the last step?

activities.title: How Many Apples?
activities.skill: Listening for numbers in a math story
activities.directions: Listen to the math story. Choose the numbers you hear.
activities.prompt: Fill in the numbers from Kofi's story.
activities.script: Kofi has 5 red apples. He has 3 green apples. He has 8 apples in all.
vocabulary: the total when you put groups together
en total: lo que hay al juntar los grupos
activities.correct: Yes! 5 red and 3 green make 8 in all. 5 + 3 = 8.
activities.hint: Listen for the color word, then the number before it.
activities.support: Use counters: put out 5 red and 3 green. Count them all together.
activities.extension: Make your own story: ___ has ___ cats and ___ dogs. How many in all?
wida: Inform: identify numbers in an oral math story

teacher.use: Math warm-up for addition language.
teacher.function: Process numbers and the phrase "in all" in an oral word problem.
teacher.lower: Read twice slowly; hold up fingers for each number.
teacher.challenge: Change to a subtraction story: Kofi ate 2. How many are left?
teacher.noTech: Students use cubes to build the story as you read.
teacher.prompt: What does "in all" mean?

activities.title: Water or Land?
activities.skill: Sorting animals by habitat from an oral description
activities.directions: Listen to your teacher. Sort each animal: does it live in water or on land?
activities.prompt: Where does each animal live?
activities.script: A fish, a whale, and an octopus live in the water. A cow, a horse, and a rabbit live on land.
vocabulary: to have a home in a place
vivir: tener casa en un lugar
tierra: el suelo, no el agua
activities.correct: Nice sorting! Fish, whales, and octopuses live in water. Cows, horses, and rabbits live on land.
activities.hint: The teacher says three animals, then where they live. Listen for "in the water" and "on land."
activities.support: Make two piles with your hands: water on one side, land on the other. Move each animal as you hear it.
activities.extension: Name one more animal. Does it live in water or on land?
wida: Inform: classify animals from spoken information

teacher.use: Science: animal habitats.
teacher.function: Classify information heard in an oral description.
teacher.lower: Read one sentence at a time; sort after each sentence.
teacher.challenge: Ask about a frog: Where does it live? (both — a good talk question).
teacher.noTech: Use animal picture cards and two hoops on the floor.
teacher.prompt: Which animal was the hardest? Why?

activities.title: Who Am I?
activities.skill: Identifying a community helper from a clue
activities.directions: Listen to a community helper talk about her job. Choose her job.
activities.prompt: What is Ms. Haddad's job?
activities.script: Hello, I am Ms. Haddad. I help sick dogs and cats feel better.
vocabulary: enfermo: que no se siente bien
to make things better for someone
ayudar: hacer las cosas mejor para alguien
activities.correct: Yes! Ms. Haddad is an animal doctor, also called a veterinarian. She helps sick dogs and cats.
activities.hint: Listen for WHO she helps.
activities.support: Act it out: who puts out fires? who brings letters? who helps sick pets?
activities.extension: Tell a partner about a helper in your community: He or she helps ___.
wida: Inform: identify a job from a description

teacher.use: Social studies: community helpers and jobs.
teacher.function: Identify a person's role from a spoken description.
teacher.lower: Read twice; bark like a dog to support meaning.
teacher.challenge: Students write their own "Who am I?" clue.
teacher.noTech: Play as a guessing game with job cards.
teacher.prompt: What words helped you know her job?

activities.title: Mei's Mitten
activities.skill: Identifying a character's feeling at the end of a story
activities.directions: Listen to a short story about Mei. Choose how she feels at the end.
activities.prompt: How does Mei feel at the end of the story?
activities.script: Mei lost her red mitten. She looked everywhere. Then she found it in her backpack, and she smiled.
vocabulary: encontró: lo vio otra vez después de buscar
activities.correct: Yes! She found her mitten and smiled, so she feels happy.
activities.hint: The question asks about the END. Listen to the last part of the story.
activities.support: Show a sad face for "lost" and a happy face for "found." Which face is at the end?
activities.extension: How did Mei feel at the BEGINNING? Tell a partner and give a reason.
wida: Narrate: identify a character's feeling and the clue

teacher.use: Language arts: character feelings in a simple narrative.
teacher.function: Infer a feeling from an action at the end of a story.
teacher.lower: Read twice and make faces with the story.
teacher.challenge: Ask students to tell how Mei's feeling changed and why.
teacher.noTech: Use feeling cards; students hold up one.
teacher.prompt: What did Mei do that showed her feeling?

activities.title: Who Read More?
activities.skill: Comparing two numbers heard in a short story
activities.directions: Listen to two students talk about reading. Choose the answer.
activities.prompt: Who read more pages?
activities.script: Diego read 12 pages last night. Amara read 20 pages last night.

options.text: They read the same number of pages.

vocabulary: the sheets of paper in a book
páginas: las hojas de un libro
look at how things are the same or different
comparar: ver en qué se parecen o se diferencian
activities.correct: Yes! Amara read 20 pages. 20 is greater than 12, so Amara read more.
activities.hint: Listen for each name and the number after it. Then compare the two numbers.
activities.support: Write the two numbers you hear. Which number is bigger?
activities.extension: How many more pages did Amara read? (20 − 12 = ?)
wida: Language of Math: more, greater than

teacher.use: Math: comparing numbers with oral language.
teacher.function: Compare quantities heard in an oral statement.
teacher.lower: Read twice; write 12 and 20 on the board as you read.
teacher.challenge: Ask for the difference: how many more?
teacher.noTech: Use a number line on the floor.
teacher.prompt: How did you know which number was greater?

B.studentGoal: I can follow steps, reasons, and details in short school talks.

info.headline: Follow the steps and find the reasons.
info.summary: Level B is for students who understand everyday English and are growing their school English. You will hear three to six sentences, like a morning announcement, a science explanation, or a math story. Listen for order words (first, after that, finally), time words (long ago, later, today), and cause words (because, so, but) to connect ideas.
canDo: I can put the steps of a process or a story in order.
I can tell the cause and the effect when I hear because or so.
I can use numbers I hear to solve a math problem.
I can sort examples using a definition my teacher says.

categories.title: Steps and Sequence
categories.desc: Track first, next, after that, and finally in procedures, life cycles, and history.

categories.title: Cause and Effect
categories.desc: Listen for because, so, and but to find reasons and results.

categories.title: Math and Science Talk
categories.desc: Use numbers and science words you hear to solve and sort.

categories.title: Important Details
categories.desc: Catch several details in a school talk.

activities.title: Walk to the New Library
activities.skill: Following a route with position and sequence words on a map
activities.directions: Look at the picture of the town map. Listen as the teacher tells the class how to walk to the new library. Then choose the library.
activities.prompt: Which building is the new library?

picture.alt: A town map. Oak Street runs across the middle. Under the street are the school, the park, a building with a star, and a building with a heart. Above the street are a building with a moon, the fire station, and a building with a sun.

activities.script: Today our class is walking to the new library. First, we leave the school and walk along Oak Street. Next, we walk past the park. The library is the building right after the park. It is across the street from the fire station.
vocabulary: going by something and beyond it
pasar por: ir al lado de algo y seguir
on the other side of the street
enfrente de: al otro lado de la calle
moving beside a road or line
a lo largo de: moverse junto a una calle o línea
frames: The library is right after the ___.
It is across the street from the ___.
activities.correct: Yes! The star building is right after the park and across the street from the fire station. You used two clues together.
activities.hint: Trace the route with your finger: school, then the park. Which building comes right after the park? Check: is it across from the fire station?
activities.support: Two clues must BOTH be true: (1) right after the park, (2) across from the fire station. Test each building.
activities.extension: Give a partner directions from the school to the building with the sun. Use past and across from.

teacher.use: Social studies map skills and community places.
teacher.function: Follow multi-step oral directions; integrate two location clues.
teacher.lower: Read one sentence at a time and let students trace on the map.
teacher.onLevel: Read once; students trace while listening.
teacher.challenge: Students write directions to another building for a partner.
teacher.noTech: Print the map; students draw the route with a crayon.
teacher.prompt: Which clue ruled out the heart building?

activities.title: Which Step of the Water Cycle?
activities.skill: Identifying a science process from a description
activities.directions: Look at the picture of the water cycle. Listen to the teacher explain one step. Choose the name of that step.
activities.prompt: Which step of the water cycle did the teacher explain?

picture.alt: The water cycle. The sun shines on a lake. Wavy arrows show water rising from the lake into the sky. Clouds form over a mountain, rain falls on the mountain, and a river flows back down into the lake.

activities.script: The sun shines on the lake all day. The sun heats the water. When water gets warm, some of it changes into a gas called water vapor. We cannot see water vapor, but it rises up into the sky.

options.text: Condensation: vapor cools and makes clouds
Evaporation: water heats up and rises as a gas
Collection: water flows back into lakes

vocabulary: when liquid water heats up and becomes a gas
evaporación: cuando el agua líquida se calienta y se vuelve gas
water as a gas in the air
vapor de agua: agua en forma de gas en el aire
frames: The sun heats the water, so it ___.
activities.correct: Correct! Heat from the sun turns water into vapor that rises. That is evaporation.
activities.hint: Listen for what the sun does to the water, and which way the water goes: up or down?
activities.support: Find the wavy arrows in the picture. They go UP from the lake. Which step goes up?
activities.extension: Explain what happens NEXT, when the water vapor cools high in the sky.
wida: Explain: identify a process from cause-and-effect language

teacher.use: Science: water cycle (grade 3–5 earth science).
teacher.function: Identify a process from a spoken explanation with cause and effect.
teacher.lower: Pause after each sentence and point to the matching part of the picture.
teacher.challenge: Students explain condensation and precipitation in order.
teacher.noTech: Draw the cycle on the board; students point to the step.
teacher.prompt: What does the sun cause in this step?

activities.title: The Bean Plant Experiment
activities.skill: Sequencing steps of a science experiment
activities.directions: Listen to Ms. Nguyen describe the class science experiment. Put the steps in order.
activities.prompt: In what order did the class do the experiment?
activities.script: Our class did a plant experiment. First, we put soil in two cups. Next, we planted three bean seeds in each cup. After that, we put one cup in a sunny window and the other cup in a dark closet. Finally, we watered both cups every day and measured the plants on Friday.

items.text: Put one cup in the sun and one in the dark.
Water every day and measure on Friday.
Plant bean seeds in each cup.

vocabulary: a test to find out something
find out how long or tall something is
medir: averiguar qué tan largo o alto es algo
después de eso: lo que sigue
activities.correct: Excellent! Soil, seeds, sun and dark, then water and measure. The order words guided you.
activities.hint: Listen for first, next, after that, and finally. Each one starts a step.
activities.support: Hold up one finger for each order word as you listen again.
activities.extension: Predict: Which plant will grow taller? Why?
wida: Narrate: sequence steps of a procedure

teacher.use: Science procedures and sequence language.
teacher.function: Sequence a four-step procedure from oral description.
teacher.lower: Read twice; show step cards one at a time.
teacher.challenge: Ask why the class used two cups (a fair test).
teacher.noTech: Students arrange step cards on desks.
teacher.prompt: Why did the class put one cup in the dark?

activities.title: Why Recess Moved
activities.skill: Identifying cause and effect in an announcement
activities.directions: Listen to the morning announcement. Choose the reason for the change.
activities.prompt: Why is recess on the blacktop today?
activities.script: Good morning, third, fourth, and fifth grades. It rained all night, so the field is very muddy. Because of the mud, recess will be on the blacktop today, not on the field. Please wear your sneakers. Thank you!

options.text: Because the field is being painted
Because it is too hot outside
Because there is a soccer game
Because the field is muddy from the rain

vocabulary: a causa de: palabras que dan una razón
wet and full of soft dirt
lodoso: mojado y lleno de lodo
the hard, dark ground on a playground
asfalto: el suelo duro y oscuro del patio
a word that tells a result
así que: palabra que dice un resultado
frames: Recess is on the blacktop because ___.
activities.correct: Yes! It rained all night, so the field is muddy. That is the cause. Moving recess is the effect.
activities.hint: Listen for "so" and "because of." They connect a cause to what happens.
activities.support: Make a chain: rain → mud → blacktop. Which part is the reason?
activities.extension: Say the cause and the effect: The cause is ___. The effect is ___.

teacher.use: School announcements; cause-and-effect language.
teacher.function: Identify cause and effect signaled by so and because.
teacher.lower: Pause after "so" and ask what happened.
teacher.onLevel: Read once at a natural pace.
teacher.challenge: Students write an announcement that uses so and because.
teacher.noTech: Read aloud; students show a cause card and an effect card.
teacher.prompt: Which word told you the result?

activities.title: Boxes of Markers
activities.skill: Understanding a multiplication word problem
activities.directions: Listen to the math story. Choose the answer.
activities.prompt: How many markers does Yusuf have in all?
activities.script: Yusuf is getting ready for art class. He has 4 boxes of markers. Each box has 6 markers. He wants to know how many markers he has altogether, so he multiplies.
vocabulary: groups with the same number in each
grupos iguales: grupos con la misma cantidad
activities.correct: Yes! 4 equal groups of 6 is 4 × 6 = 24 markers.
activities.hint: "Each box has 6" means every group is the same. How many groups?
activities.support: Draw 4 boxes. Put 6 dots in each. Count all the dots.
activities.extension: If Yusuf gives one box away, how many markers does he have?
wida: Language of Math: each, equal groups

teacher.use: Grade 3 multiplication: equal-groups language.
teacher.function: Process key math words (each, altogether, multiply) in an oral problem.
teacher.lower: Read twice; draw boxes as you read.
teacher.challenge: Students make their own equal-groups story.
teacher.noTech: Students build it with cubes.
teacher.prompt: Why did 10 not make sense?

activities.title: Library Rules
activities.skill: Identifying several details in a talk
activities.directions: Listen to Ms. Okafor talk about the school library. Choose ALL the rules she says.
activities.prompt: Which rules did Ms. Okafor tell the class?
activities.script: Welcome to the library! Here are our rules. You can borrow two books at a time. You must bring them back in two weeks. Please use a quiet voice so others can read. And remember, no food or drinks near the books.

options.text: You can borrow two books at a time.
You can bring a snack to read with.
Bring books back in two weeks.

vocabulary: take something and give it back later
pedir prestado: tomar algo y devolverlo después
what we must do or not do
reglas: lo que debemos o no debemos hacer
activities.correct: Yes! Borrow two books, bring them back in two weeks, and use a quiet voice. Food is NOT allowed.
activities.hint: Three answers are rules. One choice breaks a rule, and one has the wrong number.
activities.support: Count on your fingers as you hear each rule. How many rules did you count?
activities.extension: Why is there a rule about food near books? Explain to a partner.
wida: Inform: identify multiple details in an oral presentation

teacher.use: Library orientation; school rules.
teacher.function: Identify multiple stated details and reject contradictions.
teacher.lower: Read twice; stop after each rule.
teacher.challenge: Ask students to explain the reason for each rule.
teacher.noTech: Students show thumbs up/down for each statement read aloud.
teacher.prompt: Which choice had the wrong number?

activities.title: Solid, Liquid, or Gas?
activities.skill: Classifying examples from a science explanation
activities.directions: Listen to the science lesson about matter. Sort each example.
activities.prompt: Is each example a solid, a liquid, or a gas?
activities.script: All matter has three main states. A solid keeps its own shape, like a rock or an ice cube. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, like milk or juice. A gas spreads out to fill any space, like the air inside a balloon or the steam from hot soup.

C.studentGoal: I can understand the main idea of a longer talk and use clues to make inferences.

info.headline: Find the big idea and read between the lines.
info.summary: Level C is for students who understand a lot of school English. You will hear mini-lessons, class discussions, stories, and announcements of six to ten sentences. Some answers are not said directly: you put clues together, find the main idea or theme, take notes, and decide which speaker used which evidence.
canDo: I can tell the main idea of a short science or history talk.
I can put clues together to make an inference.
I can tell a speaker's opinion and the evidence that supports it.
I can take notes and use new definitions on new examples.

activities.title: Busy Bees: The Main Idea
activities.skill: Identifying the main idea of a science mini-lecture
activities.directions: Listen to a short science talk about bees and flowers. Then choose the main idea of the whole talk.
activities.prompt: What is the main idea of the talk?
activities.script: Have you ever watched a bee visit a flower? The bee is looking for food. Flowers make a sweet liquid called nectar, and bees drink it. While the bee drinks, a yellow powder called pollen sticks to its fuzzy body. When the bee flies to the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off. Moving pollen from flower to flower is called pollination. Pollination helps plants make seeds, so new plants can grow. Without bees and other pollinators, many fruits and vegetables could not grow.

options.text: Bees drink nectar because it is sweet.
Bees help plants make seeds by carrying pollen from flower to flower.
Some fruits are sweeter than others.

vocabulary: what the whole talk is mostly about
idea principal: de qué trata mayormente toda la charla
polen: polvo amarillo que hacen las flores
moving pollen from flower to flower so plants make seeds
polinización: llevar polen de flor en flor para que las plantas hagan semillas
néctar: líquido dulce dentro de las flores
frames: One detail is ___, but the main idea is ___.
listenFor: the topic in the first sentences
the key term the speaker defines
the reason it matters at the end
activities.correct: Yes! Nectar and yellow pollen are details. The big idea is that bees help plants make seeds through pollination.
activities.hint: A main idea covers the WHOLE talk. A detail is only one small part. Which answer connects most of the sentences?
activities.support: Ask yourself: Why did the speaker tell me about nectar and pollen? What were all those details building to?
activities.extension: Explain why farmers might care about bees. Use the word pollination.
wida: Inform: identify the main idea of an oral explanation

teacher.use: Science: plant reproduction and pollinators (grades 3–4).
teacher.function: Distinguish main idea from details in an extended oral explanation.
teacher.lower: Read twice; after the first reading, list the details on the board together.
teacher.onLevel: Read once at a natural pace.
teacher.challenge: Students summarize the talk in two sentences.
teacher.noTech: Read aloud; students sort detail cards from a main-idea card.
teacher.prompt: Which answer was a true detail but not the main idea?

activities.title: Energy in a Meadow

activities.script: Every living thing needs energy to live and grow. In a food chain, energy starts with the Sun. In this meadow, grass uses sunlight to make its own food. A grasshopper eats the grass and gets energy. Then a frog catches the grasshopper. Finally, a hawk eats the frog. Each arrow in a food chain points from the food to the animal that eats it. That shows the energy moving.

frames: Energy moves from the ___ to the ___.

activities.correct: Yes! Grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk. The grass is the producer, and energy moves up the chain.
activities.hint: Start with the plant. It uses sunlight to make food. Then ask: who eats it?
activities.support: Make a chain of "eats" sentences: The grasshopper eats ___. The frog eats ___. The hawk eats ___.
activities.extension: What might happen to the frogs if all the grasshoppers disappeared? Explain.

activities.title: The Water Bottle Debate
activities.skill: Following an argument and a response to another view
activities.directions: Listen to a class discussion about water bottles. Then answer the question.
activities.prompt: How does Sofía respond when Daniel says some students forget their water bottles?
activities.script: Sofía said, "I think our school should stop selling water in plastic bottles." Mr. Lee asked, "Why do you think that?" Sofía answered, "Our class counted the bottles in the cafeteria trash. In just one day, we found 85 plastic bottles! Many plastic bottles are never recycled, so they end up in landfills or in the ocean." Then Daniel said, "But some students forget to bring a water bottle from home." Sofía nodded. "That's true. So the school could put in a water fountain that fills reusable bottles, and keep some extra bottles in the office."

She says Daniel is wrong and stops talking.
She agrees the school should keep selling plastic bottles.

activities.hint: Listen for the word "But" from Daniel. Then listen to what Sofía says right after.
activities.support: Sofía's opinion → her evidence (85 bottles) → Daniel's concern → Sofía's solution. Which part does the question ask about?
activities.extension: What evidence did Sofía use to support her opinion? Say it in one sentence.

activities.script: This animal is called the fennec fox. It is a small fox with very large ears. Its big ears help it give off body heat, so it can stay cool. Its fur is a light, sandy color, which helps it hide. The fennec fox sleeps in an underground burrow during the hot day. It hunts at night, when the air is cooler. It can go a long time without drinking, because it gets water from the food it eats.

activities.title: Harriet Tubman's Journeys
activities.skill: Identifying accurate details in a history talk
activities.directions: Listen to a short history talk about Harriet Tubman. Choose ALL the facts the speaker says.
activities.prompt: Which facts about Harriet Tubman did you hear?
activities.script: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland around 1822. In 1849, she escaped and traveled north to Philadelphia, where she could live in freedom. But she did not just stay safe. She went back to Maryland about thirteen times to guide others to freedom. She led about seventy people, including members of her own family. She used the Underground Railroad. It was not a real railroad with trains. It was a secret network of people and safe houses that helped people escape. Later, during the Civil War, she worked as a nurse and a scout.

options.text: The Underground Railroad was a real train under the ground.
She went back about thirteen times to guide others.
She was born in New York.
She worked as a nurse and a scout in the Civil War.

frames: One fact is that Harriet Tubman ___.

activities.correct: Yes! Born in Maryland, escaped to Philadelphia, returned about thirteen times, and served as a nurse and scout. The Underground Railroad was a secret network, not a train.
activities.hint: Two choices are NOT true. One of them is a common mistake the speaker corrected. Listen for "It was not."
activities.support: Make a timeline as you listen: born → escaped → went back → Civil War.
activities.extension: Why do you think Harriet Tubman went back so many times? Explain with a detail.

activities.title: Why Is One Fourth Bigger?
activities.skill: Understanding a math explanation
activities.directions: Listen to the teacher explain how to compare two fractions. Then choose the reason she gives.
activities.prompt: According to the teacher, why is one fourth greater than one eighth?
activities.script: Let's compare one fourth and one eighth. Imagine two pizzas that are exactly the same size. We cut the first pizza into 4 equal slices. We cut the second pizza into 8 equal slices. When you cut the same size whole into more pieces, each piece gets smaller. So one slice from the first pizza is bigger than one slice from the second pizza. That means one fourth is greater than one eighth, even though 8 is a bigger number than 4.

options.text: Because 8 is a bigger number than 4.
Because the two pizzas are different sizes.
Because when a whole is cut into fewer equal pieces, each piece is bigger.
Because the first pizza has more toppings.

vocabulary: decide which is greater or less
comparar: decidir cuál es mayor o menor
the bottom number; how many equal parts in the whole
denominador: el número de abajo; cuántas partes iguales hay en el entero
frames: More pieces means each piece is ___.
activities.correct: Exactly! Same size whole, fewer pieces, so each piece is bigger. One fourth is greater than one eighth.
activities.hint: Be careful: the teacher said the pizzas are the SAME size. Listen to what happens when you cut into more pieces.
activities.support: Fold one paper strip into 4 parts and another into 8. Compare one part from each.
activities.extension: Which is greater: one third or one sixth? Explain using the teacher's reason.
wida: Language of Math: compare, greater than, equal parts

activities.title: Kwame Fixes His Bike

activities.script: Kwame's bike had a flat tire and a loose chain. He wanted to buy a new bike, but his grandfather said, "Let's try to fix it first." On Saturday, they took the tire off together. The first patch they tried did not work, and air leaked out again. Kwame felt frustrated and wanted to quit. His grandfather smiled and said, "Every fixer makes mistakes." They tried a new patch and tightened the chain, and the bike was ready. Kwame rode it around the block, feeling proud.

If you keep trying and work together, you can solve a problem.
Bikes are too hard to fix.
Grandparents always know the answer right away.

activities.correct: Yes! Kwame wanted to quit, but he and his grandfather kept trying together. The theme is about persistence and teamwork.
activities.hint: Think about how Kwame changes from the middle to the end. What did he learn?

activities.title: Why the Moon Changes

activities.prompt: Complete the notes about the Moon's phases.
activities.script: Why does the Moon seem to change shape? The Moon does not make its own light. Instead, it reflects light from the Sun, like a mirror. The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. When we see the whole lit side, we call it a full moon. When we cannot see the lit side at all, it is a new moon. It takes the Moon about one month to go through all of its phases.

activities.title: Weathering, Erosion, Deposition
activities.skill: Applying science definitions to new examples
activities.directions: Listen to the lesson about how land changes. Then sort each example. Some examples are new, so use the definitions.
activities.prompt: Is each example weathering, erosion, or deposition?
activities.script: Today we will learn three words that describe how land changes over time. Weathering is when rock is broken into smaller pieces. For example, water freezes in a crack, expands, and splits the rock. Erosion is when those pieces are carried away by water, wind, or ice. A river carrying sand downstream is erosion. Deposition is when the moving water or wind slows down and drops the pieces in a new place. When a river reaches the ocean, it slows down and drops sand and mud, and that builds new land.

items.text: Ice in a crack splits a rock.
A river drops mud where it meets the ocean.
Tree roots grow and crack a big rock.
Wind blows sand off the top of a dune.
Waves leave sand and shells on a beach.

vocabulary: meteorización: romper la roca en pedazos más pequeños
carrying pieces of rock or soil away
erosión: llevarse pedazos de roca o tierra
dropping pieces in a new place
sedimentación: dejar los pedazos en un lugar nuevo
se expande: se hace más grande
frames: ___ is weathering because the rock breaks.
___ is erosion because the pieces move away.
activities.correct: Great thinking! Breaking = weathering, moving = erosion, dropping = deposition. You applied the definitions to new examples.
activities.hint: Ask one question for each example: Is the rock BREAKING, MOVING, or being DROPPED?
activities.support: Use three hand motions: break (snap), move (push), drop (open hand). Act out each example.
activities.extension: A heavy rain washes soil from a garden into the street. Which steps happen? Explain.
wida: Explain: apply definitions to classify new examples

teacher.use: Science: Earth's surface changes (grade 4).
teacher.function: Apply orally presented definitions to classify new examples.
teacher.lower: Read twice; write each definition on the board as a key word: break, move, drop.
teacher.challenge: Students create one new example for each category.
teacher.noTech: Three labeled hoops; students sort example cards.
teacher.prompt: Which example was not in the lesson, and how did you sort it?

activities.title: Student Council Choice
activities.skill: Identifying a speaker's supporting evidence
activities.directions: Listen to a student council meeting. Two students share different ideas. Then answer the question.
activities.prompt: Which reason does Ji-woo use to support her idea?
activities.script: The student council has 100 dollars to spend. Omar said, "I think we should buy new soccer balls, because the old ones are flat." Ji-woo disagreed. She said, "I think we should build a buddy bench. A buddy bench is a place to sit when you need someone to play with. Last week, we did a survey. Forty-two out of sixty students said they sometimes have no one to play with at recess. Soccer balls only help students who play soccer, but a buddy bench could help everyone feel included." Omar said, "That's a good point. Maybe we can ask the PTA for soccer balls."

options.text: The old soccer balls are flat.
A buddy bench costs less than 100 dollars.
A survey showed 42 of 60 students sometimes have no one to play with.
The PTA will build the bench for free.

vocabulary: asking many people the same question
encuesta: hacer la misma pregunta a muchas personas
no estuvo de acuerdo: tuvo otra opinión
give reasons that make an idea stronger
apoyar: dar razones que hacen una idea más fuerte
activities.correct: Yes! Ji-woo used survey data: 42 of 60 students. Numbers from a survey are strong evidence.
activities.hint: Two speakers give reasons. Make sure you choose JI-WOO's reason, not Omar's.
activities.support: Make a T-chart: Omar's idea and reason | Ji-woo's idea and reason.
activities.extension: Which idea would you choose? Give a reason and evidence.
wida: Argue: identify a claim and supporting evidence

teacher.use: Argument and civic language: student government.
teacher.function: Attribute claims and evidence to the correct speaker.
teacher.lower: Read twice with two voices; pause after each speaker.
teacher.challenge: Students calculate: is 42 out of 60 more or less than half?
teacher.noTech: Role-play the meeting; the class votes with reasons.
teacher.prompt: Why is "the old balls are flat" the wrong answer?

activities.title: Samir's Conclusion
activities.skill: Drawing a conclusion from a science conversation
activities.directions: Listen to Ms. Rivera and Samir talk about his science project. Then choose the best conclusion.
activities.prompt: What will Samir most likely write as his conclusion?
activities.script: Ms. Rivera asked, "Samir, tell me about your results." Samir said, "I planted bean seeds in two cups. I gave both cups the same soil and the same amount of water. One cup was in the window, and one cup was in the closet." Ms. Rivera asked, "What did you notice?" Samir said, "The plant in the window is tall and green. The plant in the closet is short, thin, and yellow." Ms. Rivera said, "Everything was the same except one thing. What was different?" Samir smiled. "Only the light!"

options.text: Bean plants need light to grow healthy and green.
Bean plants need more water in a closet.
Bean plants grow best in the dark.

vocabulary: resultados: lo que pasó en un experimento
what you learned from the results
conclusión: lo que aprendiste de los resultados
activities.correct: Yes! Soil and water were the same. Only the light was different, so light made the difference.
activities.hint: Ms. Rivera asks what was DIFFERENT. The answer to that question is the key to the conclusion.
activities.support: Same: soil, water. Different: window or closet. Result: green or yellow. What caused the change?
activities.extension: Plan a new test: How could Samir test whether water amount matters?
wida: Explain: draw a conclusion from evidence

teacher.use: Science practices: fair tests and conclusions (grades 3–5).
teacher.function: Draw a conclusion by connecting variables to results in a conversation.
teacher.lower: Read twice with two voices; chart same/different on the board.
teacher.challenge: Students explain why a fair test changes only one thing.
teacher.noTech: Act out the conversation; students write the conclusion on a card.
teacher.prompt: Why are the soil and water clues important?
